passages.happening:
“Some time later God tested Abraham and said to him, ‘Abraham!’ ‘Here I am,’ he answered” (verse 1).

Then comes the command. “Take your son,” God said, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
The very first words tell the reader what Abraham does not know: this is a test. A test in the Bible is a trial that shows what is in a person's heart. The reader is let in on it from the start. Abraham is not.

Listen to how the command is built. ‘Your son.’ ‘Your only son.’ ‘Isaac.’ ‘Whom you love.’ Each phrase presses closer, until the name comes, and then love. This is the first time the Bible uses the word ‘love’. It is a father's love for his son.

‘Only son’ is strange, since Abraham has two sons. But Ishmael has just been sent away (21:14), and God has said that Abraham's family will be counted through Isaac (21:12). Isaac is the only son left at home, and the only son of the promise.

‘Go’ is the same unusual Hebrew phrase God used in 12:1, when he told Abram to leave his country and go ‘to the land I will show you’. That first call cut Abraham off from his past. This one seems to cut him off from his future.

A burnt offering was a sacrifice burned whole on an altar, given entirely to God. The worshiper kept nothing. Moriah is not named anywhere else in Genesis. Where it was is uncertain (see the note on verses 9-14).

Notice what the text does not tell us. It does not say what Abraham felt. It does not say what he thought. It gives only what he did.
passages.later:
Israel's law forbids child sacrifice outright: “You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech” (Leviticus 18:21). Moses says the nations around Israel “even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods”, and Israel must never worship God that way (Deuteronomy 12:31).

The prophets go further. When people in Judah burned their children, God said through Jeremiah that it was “something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). Micah asks, “Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression?” and answers that God wants us “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:7-8).

Israel's law also said that God has a claim on every firstborn, but it is met by redemption, a price paid instead: “every firstborn of your sons you must redeem” (Exodus 13:13).
passages.hard:
How could God command this? This is one of the hardest questions in the Bible, and it should be faced, not hurried past.

The objection at its strongest goes like this. A good God would never tell a father to kill his child, not even as a test. If he could, how could anyone trust his goodness? And a story that praises a father for being ready to do it seems dangerous. The philosopher Immanuel Kant argued in The Conflict of the Faculties (1798) that Abraham should have refused: he could be sure it was wrong to kill his innocent son, but he could never be sure that the voice was God's. Many thoughtful people, believers among them, have felt the force of this.

Three things in the Bible itself should be said plainly. First, God does not want child sacrifice. The law and the prophets forbid it and condemn it, and God says it never entered his mind (Jeremiah 7:31). Second, the story tells the reader at the start that this is a test, and God stops it before Isaac is harmed. Third, it ends with a ram offered in the boy's place. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, think part of its point is that the God of Abraham is not like the gods who demanded children.

These answers do not make every difficulty disappear. Readers still differ on how to weigh the command against how it ends. The text does not ask anyone to pretend otherwise.

One thing must be said without any doubt. No one today is told by God to harm a child, or anyone else. This story has never been read in Jewish or Christian teaching as permission to hurt a child. If you hear a voice, or have a thought, telling you to harm a child or anyone else, do not act on it. Seek help at once: tell someone you trust, a doctor, or a pastor, today. If anyone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The story begins by telling you it is a test, so you can watch what Abraham does with what he loves most. Ask what you love most, even among good gifts. Then ask whether you trust God more than the gift.

passages.happening:
“So Abraham got up early the next morning” (verse 3). He saddles his donkey, takes two servants and Isaac, splits the wood, and sets out.

“On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance” (verse 4). He tells the servants to stay with the donkey: “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you” (verse 5).

He puts the wood on Isaac and carries the fire and the knife himself, “and the two of them walked on together” (verse 6).

Isaac speaks: “My father!” “Here I am, my son,” Abraham answers. “The fire and the wood are here,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” (verse 7).

“Abraham answered, ‘God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.’ And the two walked on together” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Three days is a long time to walk toward something like this. The text says nothing about those days. No words, no feelings, only the road. The silence is part of the story.

The fire was probably live coals carried in a pot. The BSB calls the knife ‘the sacrificial knife’.

How old is Isaac? Genesis does not say. He is called ‘the boy’, a word used for a young child but also for a youth; Joseph is called by it at seventeen (37:2). He is old enough to carry a load of wood up a mountain. Later Jewish tradition gave him various ages, some of them grown.

Listen to Abraham's words to the servants: ‘we will return’. Is he hiding the truth, or does he hope against hope? The text does not say. The New Testament reads it as hope (Hebrews 11:19, below).

Then comes the only recorded conversation between Abraham and Isaac in the Bible. ‘My father.’ ‘Here I am, my son.’ Abraham answered God with ‘Here I am’ in verse 1. Now he answers his son the same way. Isaac's question is the question of the whole chapter: where is the lamb?

Abraham's answer can be read two ways at once. It can be a father protecting his son from the truth. It can be faith, trusting that God will do something no one can see yet. ‘Provide’ here is the Hebrew word ‘see’: God will see to it. The words ‘the two of them walked on together’ come before and after the question. Whatever Abraham knew, they went on side by side.
passages.later:
Hebrews explains Abraham's hope: “Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death” (Hebrews 11:19).

John the Baptist gives the answer Christians hear to Isaac's question: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).

Many Christian readers have also noticed that Isaac carries the wood up the hill, as Jesus would carry his cross: “Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull” (John 19:17). The New Testament does not draw that link itself. It is a picture later Christian writers saw.
passages.asks: Isaac asked, ‘Where is the lamb?’ and his father said God would see to it. Ask what question you are carrying up the hill with no answer yet. Then notice that the two walked on together, still trusting, still side by side.

passages.t: The binding, and the ram in his place
passages.happening:
At the place God had shown him, Abraham builds the altar and lays the wood. “He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood” (verse 9). He reaches out his hand and takes the knife (verse 10).

“Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven, ‘Abraham, Abraham!’ ‘Here I am,’ he replied” (verse 11). “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him,” said the angel, “for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me” (verse 12).

Abraham looks up and sees “a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns” (verse 13). He offers it “as a burnt offering in place of his son” (verse 13).

He names the place “The LORD Will Provide” (verse 14). And it is still said, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The story slows almost to a stop here. Built. Laid. Bound. Placed. Reached. Took. Every verb is one more step closer. Then the angel calls, and calls the name twice.

‘Bound’ gives this chapter its name in Jewish tradition. It is called the Akedah, from the Hebrew for ‘binding’. Traditional Jewish practice reads it on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. The ram's horn, the shofar, is blown in synagogues on that day. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16a) links it with this ram: it is blown so that God will remember the binding of Isaac in his people's favor.

‘Now I know that you fear God.’ To fear God is to trust and honor him above everything. The test showed what was in Abraham's heart.

The ram dies ‘in place of his son’. The text says it plainly. The idea of a substitute, one who takes another's place, runs through the rest of Israel's worship.

‘The LORD Will Provide’ is in Hebrew ‘the LORD will see’. Abraham told Isaac God would see to the lamb, and God did.

Where was Moriah? 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple ‘on Mount Moriah’ in Jerusalem, and Jewish and Christian tradition have long linked Abraham's mountain with that hill. It is usually linked with Jerusalem, but the text of Genesis does not say so, and some have placed it elsewhere.
passages.later:
The temple was built “in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3:1), where sacrifices were offered for centuries.

The New Testament takes this scene up three times. Hebrews: “By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar” (Hebrews 11:17). James: “Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?” (James 2:21). James means that Abraham's faith was shown to be real by what he did: “his faith was working with his actions” (James 2:22).

Paul writes of God, “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Many readers hear Genesis 22 behind those words, and behind the most famous verse of all: “He gave His one and only Son” (John 3:16).
passages.hard:
This chapter has been read by many people, in many ways, and each reading deserves to be heard.

In Jewish tradition the Akedah is read in more than one way. It is held up as the great example of faithful obedience, and it is remembered at the New Year, as the note above says. Some old readings soften the command: the rabbi Rashi (1000s AD), following an older Jewish commentary, says that God never wanted Isaac killed. God said ‘bring him up’ the mountain, and then ‘bring him down’.

Christians read it as a picture of the Father giving the Son. That is a Christian reading; Genesis does not say it. But the differences matter as much as the likeness. Isaac was spared, and a ram died in his place. God did not spare his own Son. And Jesus gave himself freely.

The Danish writer Søren Kierkegaard, in Fear and Trembling (1843), refused to make the story comfortable. He said that if Abraham's act is judged only by the ordinary rules of right and wrong, Abraham is a murderer, and that faith, if it is real, is something terrible and beyond explaining.

Muslims tell of the near-sacrifice too. In the Qur'an (sura 37) Abraham sees in a dream that he must sacrifice his son, the son agrees, and God ransoms him with a great sacrifice. The Qur'an does not name the son. Most Muslims today hold that he was Ishmael, though some early Muslim scholars said Isaac. Muslims remember this at Eid al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice. Christians and Muslims differ here, and both can speak of it with respect.
passages.asks: God stopped the knife and gave a ram in the boy's place. Ask what it means to you that God provides what you cannot. Then ask how the story changes when you remember that, on another hill, God did not spare his own Son.

passages.happening:
“And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time” (verse 15).

“By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son, I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore” (verses 16-17). His descendants will possess the gates of their enemies (verse 17). “And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice” (verse 18).

Abraham goes back to his servants, and they go together to Beersheba, where he settles (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
People swear by someone greater than themselves. God has no one greater, so he swears by himself. This is the only time in Genesis that God does this.

The promise gathers up everything God has said to Abraham since chapter 12: blessing, a great family, and blessing for all nations. Stars and sand are two pictures of a number too large to count.

‘Possess the gates of their enemies’ means to overcome them. A city's gate was its defense and the place where it was ruled.

This is the last time God speaks to Abraham in Genesis. The story ends where it began, with a promise for the whole world.

Notice verse 19. Abraham goes back to the servants. The text does not mention Isaac. Readers have wondered about that silence. The next chapters tell of Sarah's death and of finding Isaac a wife.
passages.later:
Hebrews says God swore by himself because “He had no one greater to swear by” (Hebrews 6:13), so that we might have strong hope (Hebrews 6:18).

Paul says this promise was the gospel told in advance: “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). Peter preached the promise of verse 18 in the temple (Acts 3:25).
passages.asks: God bound himself with an oath so that Abraham could be sure. Ask what promise of God you find hard to trust. Then remember that the One who made it swore by himself, because there was no one greater.

passages.t: News from Nahor's family, and Rebekah
passages.happening:
“Some time later, Abraham was told, ‘Milcah has also borne sons to your brother Nahor’” (verse 20). The names follow: Uz, Buz, Kemuel and others, and Bethuel (verses 21-22).

“And Bethuel became the father of Rebekah” (verse 23). Milcah had eight sons. Nahor's concubine, Reumah, had four more (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
After the mountain, a family list. It seems like an odd place for one, but it is there on purpose.

Nahor is Abraham's brother, who stayed behind in the north when Abraham left (11:27-31). While Abraham waited decades for one son, Nahor's family grew to twelve sons. The number twelve comes again with Ishmael's sons (25:16) and Jacob's sons.

A concubine was a wife of lower rank, often a servant. Her children counted in the family, but usually did not have the full rights of the main wife's children.

The list ends with the one name that matters for what comes next: Rebekah. She is Nahor's granddaughter. Isaac has been saved from the altar, and now the reader learns that the woman he will marry has been born. God's promise moves to the next generation.
passages.later: Rebekah's story begins in Genesis 24, when Abraham's servant travels to Nahor's town to find a wife for Isaac. Paul later names her in Romans: “Rebecca's children were conceived by one man, our father Isaac” (Romans 9:10).
passages.asks: Right after the hardest day of his life, Abraham hears ordinary family news. Ask whether you notice the quiet ways God prepares what comes next. Then ask who in your own family's story was being prepared long before you knew it.
